pairs.rationale: Both describe a morning consultation by chief priests and elders before Jesus is handed to Pilate. Matthew explicitly states their purpose of putting Him to death; Mark also names scribes and the whole council.
Both narrate Jesus being bound, led away, and handed to Pilate after the leaders' consultation. Matthew explicitly identifies Pilate as governor.

The earlier same-book account gives Judas's agreement with the chief priests for thirty silver coins. His return of those coins after the condemnation reverses that transaction; the earlier passage does not describe his regret.

Judas calls the betrayed blood innocent; Luke's centurion calls Jesus righteous after His death. Both are affirmations of Jesus' innocence in the passion narratives, from different speakers at different moments.

Both accounts relate Judas's death in connection with betrayal money, but the details differ: Matthew says he returned the coins and hanged himself; Acts describes a field acquired from wrongdoing wages and a headlong fall with bodily rupture. No combined death sequence is invented.

The same-book negotiation identifies the silver as payment to hand Jesus over. That earlier use supplies the narrative reason the priests now call it blood-price, without independently establishing the legal rule they invoke.

Both link a field to Judas's wrongdoing and blood. Matthew says the priests buy a potter's field with returned coins for strangers' burial; Acts says Judas acquired a field from wrongdoing wages. The purchaser, stated use, and sequence remain distinct.

Both explain the name Field of Blood as a publicly known result of the Judas episode. Acts additionally gives Hakeldamach in the local language; this shared name does not resolve the different purchase and death details.

The thirty silver coins and valuation language have a close comparison in Zechariah's thirty-piece wages. Matthew expressly attributes its fulfillment saying to Jeremiah; the supplied Zechariah ends with a smelting furnace in the Lord's house, not a potter's field. The attribution and wording differences remain unresolved.

Within this same chapter, the fulfillment saying's coins given for a potter's field correspond to the priests' narrated purchase of that field. This internal link identifies the narrative application, not an independent Old Testament source or a resolution of the Jeremiah attribution.
Both have Pilate ask whether Jesus is King of the Jews and Jesus reply You say it or You say so. Matthew explicitly locates Him standing before the governor.
Both present accusations by the chief priests and Jesus' refusal to answer further. Matthew also names elders; Mark places the explicit silence after Pilate's follow-up question.
Both have Pilate ask why Jesus does not answer the many accusations brought against Him. The questions draw attention to His silence rather than supplying a defense.
Both connect Jesus' continued refusal to answer with Pilate's marveling. Matthew emphasizes that He did not answer even one word and that the governor marveled greatly.
Both describe the customary release at the feast of one prisoner requested by the crowd. Matthew specifies the governor as the one following the custom.

Both introduce the imprisoned Barabbas. Matthew calls him notorious and preserves the name Jesus Barabbas; Mark calls him Barabbas and associates him with rebels who committed murder during an uprising.

Both have Pilate offer Jesus for release and the crowd directed toward Barabbas instead. Matthew explicitly presents a choice between Jesus Barabbas and Jesus called Christ; Mark's question names the King of the Jews.
Both explain Pilate's perception that the chief priests handed Jesus over from envy. Matthew's pronoun refers back to the accusers named in the narrative.

Pilate's wife calls Jesus righteous in her warning, while Luke's centurion calls Him righteous after seeing His death. The shared innocence testimony does not make Luke attest the wife's dream or message.
Both have chief priests influence the crowd to request Barabbas's release rather than Jesus. Matthew also names elders and explicitly states the aim of destroying Jesus.

Both accounts present the crowd's preference for Barabbas in the release dispute. Matthew states the governor's question as a choice of two and gives the direct answer; Mark describes the priests stirring the crowd toward that request.
Both have Pilate ask what to do with Jesus and receive the crowd's demand for crucifixion. Matthew calls Him Jesus called Christ; Mark uses the One you call the King of the Jews.
Both have Pilate question what evil Jesus has done, followed by a louder demand for crucifixion. Neither cited passage supplies an answer identifying a crime.

Both combine washing hands with disclaiming innocent blood. Deuteronomy concerns elders responding to an unsolved killing and seeking atonement; Pilate publicly disclaims responsibility before authorizing crucifixion. This comparison neither identifies the procedures as identical nor validates Pilate's claim of innocence.

Both use blood coming upon people as language of responsibility for Jesus' death. Matthew reports this crowd accepting it; Acts has leaders accuse the apostles of intending to bring His blood upon them. The comparison does not extend responsibility to all Jews or later generations.
Both narrate Barabbas being released and Jesus flogged and handed over for crucifixion. Mark explicitly relates Pilate's action to satisfying the crowd.
Both have soldiers lead Jesus into the praetorium and assemble the whole cohort. Matthew identifies them as the governor's soldiers; Mark describes the courtyard as the praetorium.

Both describe soldiers putting a royal-colored garment on Jesus for mockery. Matthew calls it a scarlet cloak after stripping Him; Mark calls it purple. The color descriptions are retained rather than harmonized.
Both narrate a thorn crown, a mocking royal salute, and kneeling before Jesus. Matthew additionally places a reed in His right hand; Mark's reed appears as the instrument used to strike His head.
Both describe soldiers spitting on Jesus and repeatedly striking His head with a reed. Mark also includes kneeling to bow before Him in the same verse.

Both conclude the soldiers' mockery by removing its garment, putting Jesus' own clothes back on Him, and leading Him out for crucifixion. Matthew's cloak and Mark's purple remain differently described.
Both identify Simon of Cyrene as the man compelled to carry Jesus' cross. Mark additionally calls him a passerby from the country and names his sons Alexander and Rufus.
Both identify Golgotha and give the meaning Place of a Skull. Matthew says they came there; Mark says they brought Jesus there.

Both describe offered wine that Jesus does not drink. Matthew specifies gall and says He tasted it before refusing; Mark specifies myrrh and says He did not take it. The mixtures and narrated actions are not made identical.
Both narrate crucifixion and the division of Jesus' garments by casting a lot. Mark explicitly states that the lot determines who takes what.
Both identify the written crucifixion charge as King of the Jews. Matthew's inscription includes This is Jesus; Mark's cited wording does not, so the inscription texts remain distinct.
Both describe two robbers crucified beside Jesus, one at His right and one at His left. The shared detail does not depend on adding Mark's absent verse 28.
Both describe passersby reviling Jesus and shaking their heads. Mark begins their spoken taunt in the same verse; Matthew continues it in the next.
Both taunts invoke destroying and rebuilding the sanctuary in three days and demand self-rescue from the cross. Matthew adds If Thou art God's Son, which is absent from Mark's cited taunt.
Both introduce mocking by chief priests together with scribes. Matthew additionally names elders; Mark says they mock among themselves and begins their speech in the same verse.
Both mock Jesus for saving others but not Himself and demand that Israel's king descend from the cross to elicit belief. Mark also calls Him the Christ and mentions seeing before believing.

The taunt about trusting God and asking God to rescue the one He desires closely recalls this edition's Greek-numbered Psalm 21:9. Matthew additionally cites Jesus' claim to be God's Son, which the psalm verse does not state.
Both say those crucified with Jesus reproached Him. This agreement is retained without importing a different account's distinction between the two condemned men.
Both describe darkness over the whole land from the sixth until the ninth hour. The shared time span is preserved without converting it into an unstated modern timetable.
Both place Jesus' loud forsakenness cry at about the ninth hour and translate it as My God, My God, why hast Thou forsaken Me. Matthew preserves Eli, Eli; Mark preserves Eloi, Eloi.
Both report nearby hearers interpreting the cry as a call to Elijah. Matthew says some standing there; Mark similarly names some standing nearby.
Both describe someone running to fill a sponge with sour wine, placing it on a reed, and offering Jesus a drink. Mark continues with the Elijah remark in the same verse.

Both contain a proposal to wait and see whether Elijah intervenes. Matthew attributes it to the rest, while Mark attaches it to the person offering the drink; save and take Him down are also distinct wordings.
Both narrate Jesus dying after a loud cry. Matthew says He released His spirit; Mark says He breathed His last, preserving the different descriptions.
Both describe the sanctuary veil torn in two from top to bottom. Matthew additionally records an earthquake and splitting rocks, details not supplied by this Mark verse.

Both associate opened tombs with restored life. Ezekiel explicitly addresses Israel's house in a restoration oracle; Matthew narrates holy people's bodies raised in the passion account. Ezekiel is an imagery comparison, not independent testimony to Matthew's particular event.
Both have a centurion identify Jesus as God's Son. Matthew includes fellow guards and fear at the earthquake and events; Mark describes the centurion's response to the way Jesus died.
Both describe women watching from a distance who followed and served Jesus in Galilee. Mark additionally mentions many other women coming with Him to Jerusalem.

Both name Mary Magdalene and a Mary associated with James among the witnesses. Matthew says James and Joseph and identifies Zebedee's sons' mother; Mark says James the Little and Joses and names Salome. No unproved identity of the third designation is imposed.

Both introduce Joseph of Arimathea approaching in the evening for the burial. Matthew calls him rich and a disciple; Mark calls him a respected council member awaiting God's kingdom and specifies Preparation.
Both have Joseph ask Pilate for Jesus' body and Pilate grant it. Mark includes Pilate checking the death with the centurion; Matthew abbreviates the exchange to the request and order.
Both describe Joseph wrapping Jesus' body in linen. Matthew specifies clean linen; Mark says Joseph bought the cloth and took the body down.
Both describe burial in a rock-cut tomb with a stone rolled to its entrance. Matthew explicitly calls it Joseph's own new tomb; those ownership and newness details are absent from this Mark verse.
Both identify Mary Magdalene and another Mary as watching the burial place. Matthew calls the second woman the other Mary and says they sit opposite; Mark calls her Mary the mother of Joses.

The opponents recall Jesus' prediction of rising after three days; the earlier same-book prediction explicitly promises resurrection on the third day. The reported after-three-days and on-the-third-day formulations remain distinct.

The feared explanation here is disciples stealing the body and claiming resurrection; the later same-book episode explicitly instructs guards to spread the stolen-body story. This traces an internal narrative development, not proof that the reported theft occurred.

The sealed stone and guard established here are confronted in the following scene by the rolled stone and guards overcome with fear. This same-book contrast concerns the narrative's security and its reversal, not an independent account of the sealing.

Both place women including Mary Magdalene at the tomb after the Sabbath on the first day. Matthew names the other Mary and the dawn; Mark names Mary mother of James and Salome, spices, and the sun having risen.

Both describe the tomb's stone rolled away. Matthew narrates an earthquake and an angel moving it; Mark has the women discover it already rolled away and does not describe the earthquake or the rolling action.

Both describe the tomb messenger in white clothing. Matthew calls him an angel with lightning-like appearance outside on the stone; Mark describes a young man in white sitting inside on the right. The locations and descriptions remain distinct.
Both tell the women not to fear or be alarmed and identify the one they seek as the crucified Jesus. Mark additionally calls Him the Nazarene.
Both say Jesus is raised and not there and direct attention to where His body had lain. Matthew adds as He said; neither passage supplies a body remaining in that place.
Both send the women to tell disciples that Jesus goes ahead to Galilee and will be seen there. Mark explicitly includes Peter and recalls what Jesus told them.

Both describe departure from the tomb with fear. Matthew adds great joy and running to report; Mark's verse 8 describes trembling, astonishment, and saying nothing to anyone. These immediate responses are not forced into identical wording or sequence.

Both describe an encounter with risen Jesus followed by a message to disciples. Matthew has women grasp His feet and worship; John centers on Mary Magdalene, her recognition, and His instruction not to cling. The participants and actions are not silently harmonized.

Both have risen Jesus send a message through a woman or women to My brothers. Matthew directs them to Galilee to see Him; John's message concerns His ascending to the Father, not a Galilee rendezvous.

The guards reporting the events are linked to the preceding same-book account of the guarded, sealed tomb. This internal continuity identifies the witnesses in the narrative rather than supplying independent confirmation of their assignment.

Both show the chief priests using silver to secure action against Jesus: earlier Judas's betrayal, here soldiers' cooperation with the proposed account. The recipients, sums, and purposes differ; the transactions are not identified as one.

The stolen-body explanation that opponents feared earlier becomes the story they now instruct the soldiers to tell. The same-book recurrence exposes the narrative's movement from an anticipated allegation to an instructed claim.

This same-chapter callback records the carrying out of the paid instruction and dissemination of the specified account. The earlier verses supply the payment and invented stolen-body story; the link does not endorse that story as a true theft report.

The disciples' journey to Galilee corresponds to Jesus' earlier promise that after being raised He would go ahead there. The earlier verse does not specify the mountain or independently narrate this meeting.

Both portray uncertainty among disciples seeing risen Jesus. Matthew combines worship with some doubting; Luke describes fear of a spirit, questions about doubts, and bodily reassurance. The scenes and reactions are compared without being declared identical.

Both speak of authority being given with universal scope. Daniel describes nations worshiping the visionary figure and an everlasting authority and kingdom; Matthew has Jesus declare all authority in heaven and earth. This is a royal-authority comparison, not a verbatim quotation.

Both commissions extend the disciples' mission universally. Matthew says make disciples of all nations and gives a triadic baptismal formula; Acts says witness to the earth's end with the Spirit's power and does not repeat that formula.

Matthew's closing assurance I am with you corresponds to its opening explanation of Emmanuel as God with us. This same-book literary connection preserves the different settings of birth-prophecy interpretation and the continuing discipleship mission.
